```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7.5,
  fig.height = 5,
  dpi = 96,
  out.width = "100%"

```

The Delphi method elicits the judgements of a panel of experts through
successive rounds of anonymous rating, interleaved with controlled feedback
on the distribution of the group's responses. The analysis of each round
typically addresses four questions: how the ratings are distributed, whether
the panel has reached consensus, whether the ratings have stabilised between
rounds, and which items should be submitted to a further round. DelphiR
provides a consistent workflow for these steps, from the import of the raw
ratings to a complete round report.

```{r setup}
library(DelphiR)
```

# Data format

DelphiR is built around a wide layout: each row contains the ratings given
by one expert, each column refers to one item, and each cell holds a numeric
rating. Empty cells denote missing ratings (item non-response).

| expert | round | indicator | E1 | E2 | E3 |
|--------|-------|-----------|----|----|----|
| EXP01  | 1     | impact    | 9  | 7  | 5  |
| EXP02  | 1     | impact    | 6  | 5  | 7  |
| EXP03  | 1     | impact    | 8  |    | 6  |

Three columns describe the context of each row:

* the expert identifier, which is required to follow the same expert across
  rounds;
* the round number (1, 2, ...);
* the indicator, such as impact or plausibility, when the same items are
  rated on more than one dimension.

The round and indicator columns are optional. When they are absent, the
table is treated as a single round and a single indicator, specified through
the `round` and `indicator` arguments. Each indicator has its own rating
scale, against which the ratings are validated.

`delphi_template()` creates an empty Excel file in this format, with a sheet
for the ratings, a sheet for the full statements of the items and a sheet of
instructions that includes the code needed to import the completed file.

```{r template, eval = FALSE}
delphi_template("my_delphi.xlsx", items = 12,
                indicators = c("impact", "probability"))
```

# Importing the ratings

Ratings can be imported from a data frame with `delphi_data()` or directly
from a CSV, TSV or Excel file with `read_delphi()`. The separator and the
decimal mark of text files are detected automatically, including the
semicolon-separated files with decimal commas produced by many European
spreadsheet applications.

```{r import-file}
path <- system.file("extdata", "delphi_round1.csv", package = "DelphiR")
r1 <- read_delphi(path, expert_col = "expert",
                  indicator = "impact", scale = c(1, 10))
r1
```

Tables referring to different rounds or indicators can be imported
separately and combined with `delphi_bind()`, for example
`delphi_bind(r1, r2)`. Alternatively, rounds and indicators can be stacked
in a single table, as in the example dataset shipped with the package, in
which fifteen experts rated eight items on impact (from 1 to 10) and
plausibility (from 1 to 100) over two rounds.

```{r import-df}
head(delphi_example)

x <- delphi_data(
  delphi_example,
  expert_col = "expert", round_col = "round", indicator_col = "indicator",
  scale = list(impact = c(1, 10), plausibility = c(1, 100))
)
x
```

Ratings outside the declared scale, non-numeric entries and duplicated
experts are reported with an informative error, so that coding mistakes are
detected before any analysis is carried out. Rows without an expert
identifier, such as summary rows with medians or quartiles added below the
data, are ignored with a warning.

## Long format

Ratings can also be supplied in long format, with one row per rating and
columns for the expert, the item and the value, and optionally the round and
the indicator. This is the format produced by most statistical software when
data are reshaped. Long tables are imported with `delphi_data_long()` or with
`read_delphi(layout = "long")`, and any `delphi_data` object can be returned
to this format with `as.data.frame()`.

```{r long}
long <- as.data.frame(x)
head(long)
x_long <- delphi_data_long(
  long, round_col = "round", indicator_col = "indicator",
  scale = list(impact = c(1, 10), plausibility = c(1, 100))
)
identical(x_long$data, x$data)
```

## Survey exports with two header rows

When each item is rated on several indicators, survey platforms and
spreadsheets often place the indicators side by side, with a first header
row naming the indicator of each column and a second row giving the item
statement above each group of columns:

|    |      | Impact            | Probability | Impact            | Probability |
|----|------|-------------------|-------------|-------------------|-------------|
| ID | Age  | 1. First statement |            | 2. Second statement |           |
| 11 | 30   | 8                 | 6           | 5                 | 4           |

Such files are read with `header_rows = 2`. Items are coded `E1`, `E2`, ...
in order of appearance, their statements are stored as labels and used in
reports, and columns without an indicator (such as `Age`) are ignored.
Indicator names can be translated or shortened with `indicator_names`.

```{r two-header, eval = FALSE}
r1 <- read_delphi(
  "study.xlsx", sheet = "ROUND_1", header_rows = 2,
  expert_col = "ID", round = 1, scale = c(1, 10),
  indicator_names = c(IMPATTO = "impact", PROBAB = "probability")
)
```

## Linked and unlinked panels

Comparisons between rounds at the level of the individual expert require
that the same expert has the same identifier in every round. This is not
the case when each round is collected with a separate questionnaire and the
identifiers are response numbers: the same number then denotes different
people. Declaring `linked = FALSE` prevents spurious pairings: retention is
not computed, and stability is assessed by comparing the rounds as
independent samples (see below). Tables imported without an expert
identifier are treated as unlinked.

# Descriptive statistics and panel participation

`summary()` gives an overview of the panel and of the median and
interquartile range (IQR) of each item by round. Items that reach consensus
are marked with an asterisk.

```{r summary}
summary(x)
```

`delphi_describe()` returns the full set of descriptive statistics, and
`delphi_panel()` the number of respondents and the retention rate in each
round.

```{r describe}
head(delphi_describe(x, indicator = "impact"))
delphi_panel(x)
```

Quartiles are computed with R's default algorithm (`type = 7`). Setting
`type = 6` reproduces the quartiles reported by SPSS and Minitab, which
facilitates comparison with studies analysed with that software.

# Consensus

Following the review of consensus measures by von der Gracht (2012), an
item is considered to have reached consensus when its IQR does not exceed
20% of the rating scale. By default, the scale is measured by its number of
points, so that the threshold corresponds to an IQR of at most 1 on a
five-point scale and at most 2 on a ten-point scale. The threshold can be
changed with `threshold`, and `relative_to = "range"` measures the scale as
its maximum minus its minimum, which is preferable for continuous scales.

```{r consensus}
cons <- delphi_consensus(x, round = 2)
cons
```

# Stability

Consensus describes the agreement of the panel within a round; stability
describes whether the ratings have ceased to change between rounds.
When the experts are linked across rounds, `delphi_stability()` compares
consecutive rounds on the experts who rated the item in both, so that
attrition is not mistaken for a change of opinion. Two criteria are
available: the Wilcoxon test (the default), under which an item is stable
when the test is not significant, and a criterion based on Scheibe, Skutsch
and Schofer (1975), under which an item is stable when the net change
between the two rating distributions does not exceed 15%. The net change is
half the sum of the absolute differences between the shares of experts in
each class of the scale, that is, the share of experts who would have to
move to turn one distribution into the other. Setting
`method = "both"` requires both conditions. With linked experts the
Wilcoxon test is the paired signed-rank test; with unlinked experts the
rounds are compared as independent samples with the rank-sum
(Mann-Whitney) test, and differences between rounds then reflect both
changes of opinion and changes in the composition of the panel.

```{r stability}
delphi_stability(x, indicator = "impact")
```

# Item status and the next round

`delphi_status()` combines consensus and stability into four categories:
*consensus* (consensus reached and stable), *unstable consensus* (consensus
reached, but ratings still changing), *stable dissent* (no consensus, but
ratings no longer changing) and *open* (neither). Items with an unstable
consensus or an open status are flagged for a further round. A stable
dissent is a substantive result: it indicates a persistent disagreement
that a further round is unlikely to resolve.

```{r status}
st <- delphi_status(x)
st
subset(st, next_round)
```

# Figures

DelphiR draws four figures with ggplot2, all available through `plot()`.
They are returned as ggplot objects and can therefore be modified with the
usual ggplot2 syntax or saved with `ggplot2::ggsave()`.

The distribution of the ratings in each round shows how the panel converges
or remains divided.

```{r fig-distribution, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(x, type = "distribution", indicator = "impact")
```

The median and IQR across rounds summarise the same information; filled
points denote consensus.

```{r fig-trend, fig.height = 5.5}
plot(x, type = "trend", indicator = "impact")
```

The consensus heat map displays the relative IQR of every item in every
round, coloured relative to the consensus threshold. Since the relative IQR
does not depend on the scale, indicators rated on different scales can be
shown side by side.

```{r fig-consensus, fig.height = 5}
plot(x, type = "consensus")
```

With two indicators, the items can be mapped by their median ratings, as in
the impact-plausibility matrices used in foresight studies.

```{r fig-map, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 7}
plot(x, type = "map")
```

# Expert comments

Delphi questionnaires usually invite the experts to justify their ratings in
a written comment. DelphiR stores the comments next to the ratings, so that
each comment can be read together with the rating given by its author. The
recommended layout has one row per comment, with the expert, the round, the
item and the text of the comment; an empty item denotes a general comment
on the questionnaire. This is the layout of the `comments` sheet of the
template, which `read_delphi()` reads with `comments_sheet = "comments"`.
Survey platforms that export one comment column per item are handled by
`delphi_add_comments(layout = "wide")`.

```{r comments-add}
head(delphi_example_comments, 3)
x <- delphi_add_comments(x, delphi_example_comments)
x
```

`delphi_comments()` lists the comments with the rating of their author on
every indicator, and its position relative to the ratings of the panel:
below the first quartile, within the interquartile range or above the third
quartile. Comments from experts outside the interquartile range present the
arguments of the minority, which the Delphi method asks the rest of the
panel to consider.

```{r comments-list}
delphi_comments(x, items = "E7", general = FALSE)
```

`delphi_comment_counts()` counts the comments received by each item, and
`plot(x, type = "comments")` shows them split by the position of their
authors.

```{r comments-counts, fig.height = 4}
delphi_comment_counts(x)
plot(x, type = "comments")
```

The analysis of the content of the comments remains a task for the
researchers. A common approach is to code each comment with one or more
themes, written in a `theme` column and separated by semicolons;
`delphi_themes()` then tabulates the themes by item or across items.
`delphi_words()` gives a first, descriptive overview of the words used in
the comments, after removing common English and Italian words.

```{r comments-themes}
delphi_themes(x, by = "theme")
delphi_words(x, top = 8)
```

# Round report

`delphi_report()` assembles the analyses above into a self-contained report
in HTML or Microsoft Word format. The report states the criteria adopted,
with references, and lists the items to be submitted to the next round. Full item statements are taken from the labels stored in the data,
as read from the items sheet of the template or from a file with two header
rows, or can be supplied through `item_labels`.

```{r report, eval = FALSE}
delphi_report(
  x,
  file = "round2_report.docx",
  title = "Delphi study on the future of work: round 2",
  author = "Research team",
  item_labels = c(
    E1 = "Remote work becomes the default arrangement for knowledge workers",
    E2 = "AI agents autonomously manage recruitment pipelines"
  )
)
```

When the data contain comments, the report includes a section on them: the
number of comments by item, the themes, the most frequent words and the
comments on the items for the next round, each with the position of its
author. Expert identifiers are never shown. All comments can be listed with
`comments = "all"`.

# Feedback for the next round

Before a further round, the experts receive the controlled feedback of the
current one. `delphi_feedback()` prepares it for the items that require a
further round, or for the items chosen with `items`: the median and the
quartiles of the panel on every indicator, whether consensus was reached,
and the comments of the experts, reported anonymously. With `file`, the
feedback is written to an HTML or Word document addressed to the experts,
which explains these statistics in plain words.

```{r feedback}
fb <- delphi_feedback(x)
fb
attr(fb, "comments")
```

```{r feedback-file, eval = FALSE}
delphi_feedback(x, file = "feedback_round3.docx")
```

# Interactive application

`run_app()` opens the same workflow in an application in the web browser,
for users who prefer not to write code. The ratings are imported by
choosing the columns of the file that hold the experts, the rounds, the
indicators and the items; rounds stored in separate sheets or files are
added one at a time, and comments can be added in either layout. The
criteria for consensus and stability are set in a sidebar and apply to every
table, figure and report. The application also writes the R code that
reproduces the analysis, so that the results can be documented and
repeated.

```{r app, eval = FALSE}
run_app()
run_app(x)   # open a study already imported in R
```

# References

Scheibe, M., Skutsch, M. and Schofer, J. (1975). Experiments in Delphi
methodology. In H. A. Linstone and M. Turoff (Eds.), *The Delphi Method:
Techniques and Applications* (pp. 262-287). Reading, MA:
Addison-Wesley.

von der Gracht, H. A. (2012). Consensus measurement in Delphi studies:
Review and implications for future quality assurance. *Technological
Forecasting and Social Change*, 79(8), 1525-1536.
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.techfore.2012.04.013
